# Scalability {#sec-scalability}

Three applications have been strong-scaled on LUMI-G from one GCD to 32 GCDs
across four nodes. This chapter reports those curves, what limits them, and
where they stop being worth extending.

## Method

All measurements are on LUMI-G, one MPI rank per GCD, double precision, I/O
disabled, from the `standard-g` and `dev-g` partitions. The reported quantity
is the **median `wall_step`** over accepted steps after a warm-up frame — the
first frames include FFT planning and first-touch allocation and are not
representative.

For a baseline of $p_0 = 1$ GCD,

$$
S(p) \;=\; \frac{t(1)}{t(p)},
\qquad
E(p) \;=\; \frac{S(p)}{p}.
$$ {#eq-scaling-defs}

Strong scaling means the global problem size is fixed while $p$ grows, so the
work per rank shrinks and the communication-to-computation ratio rises. Every
curve here must therefore fall away from ideal eventually; the useful question
is where, and why.

Raw data is committed under `data/` and the figures are regenerated from it by
`figures/make_figures.py`.

## Choosing the working point

A strong-scaling curve is only meaningful if the single-rank baseline is
genuinely compute-bound. Too small a grid and the baseline is dominated by
launch overhead, which flatters every subsequent point.

![Single-GCD sizing sweep for `tungsten_hip`. The near-linear slope on
log–log axes shows cost tracking cell count, so $768^3$ is a defensible
compute-bound baseline.](figures/scaling_sizing.svg){#fig-sizing}

| $L_x$ | Cells | Job | Median `wall_step` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 16.8 M | 21759671 | 20 ms |
| 384 | 56.6 M | 21759672 | 79 ms |
| 512 | 134 M | 21759709 | 232 ms |
| 640 | 262 M | 21759710 | 466 ms |
| 768 | 453 M | 21759720 | 847 ms |

$768^3$ was chosen as the strong-scaling grid: it is comfortably compute-bound
at one GCD and still fits in device memory.

## Strong-scaling results

![Strong-scaling speedup and parallel efficiency on LUMI-G, 1–32 GCDs. The
dotted vertical line marks one full node (8 GCDs); everything to its right is
multi-node and crosses the Slingshot
interconnect.](figures/scaling_strong.svg){#fig-strong}

### Tungsten PFC, $768^3$ {#sec-scal-tungsten}

Spectral ETD, the model of @sec-tungsten.

| GCDs | Nodes | Job | `wall_step` | Speedup | Efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 21761281 | 851 ms | 1.00 | 100% |
| 8 | 1 | 21764313 | 177 ms | 4.81 | 60% |
| 16 | 2 | 21764315 | 84 ms | 10.2 | 64% |
| 24 | 3 | 21764316 | 72 ms | 11.9 | 50% |
| 32 | 4 | 21764317 | 63 ms | 13.6 | 42% |

`SPECTRAL_CHECKSUM` at 1 and 16 GCDs agrees to about $10^{-12}$ relative, so
the speedup is not being bought with a changed answer.

The efficiency **rises** from 8 to 16 GCDs (60% → 64%). That is not noise and
not a scaling anomaly: it is a decomposition effect. Going to two nodes changes
the pencil/slab layout the transform uses, and the two-node layout happens to
suit this grid better than the eight-rank single-node one. It is a reminder
that FFT scaling on a fixed grid is sensitive to how the decomposition divides
the axes, not only to rank count.

### Heat3D spectral HIP, $768^3$

Implicit Euler in Fourier space, two transforms per step — the spectral driver
of @sec-heat3d.

| GCDs | Nodes | Job | `wall_step` | Speedup | Efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 21773962 | 416 ms | 1.00 | 100% |
| 2 | 1 | 21774367 | 204 ms | 2.04 | 102% |
| 4 | 1 | 21774368 | 127 ms | 3.29 | 82% |
| 8 | 1 | 21774369 | 88 ms | 4.74 | 59% |
| 16 | 2 | 21773966 | 50 ms | 8.34 | 52% |
| 24 | 3 | 21773967 | 39 ms | 10.6 | 44% |
| 32 | 4 | 21773968 | 34 ms | 12.2 | 38% |

The 102% at two GCDs is superlinear and should be read as a cache/occupancy
effect at the boundary of measurement precision, not as a real gain.

Checksums at 1 and 16 GCDs agree to about $3\times10^{-16}$.

### Heat3D finite difference HIP, $512^3$

Device halo exchange plus stencil, second order — the FD driver of
@sec-heat3d, on the same PDE as the spectral driver above.

| GCDs | Nodes | Job | `wall_step` | Speedup | Efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 21761036 | 5.91 ms | 1.00 | 100% |
| 8 | 1 | 21761037 | 0.951 ms | 6.22 | 78% |
| 16 | 2 | 21761038 | 0.567 ms | 10.4 | 65% |
| 24 | 3 | 21761039 | 0.476 ms | 12.4 | 52% |
| 32 | 4 | 21761042 | 0.394 ms | 15.0 | 47% |

Checksums at 1 and 16 GCDs agree to about $5\times10^{-15}$.

## Reading the comparison

The finite-difference curve is the best of the three at every rank count — 78%
efficiency at one node against 59% for the spectral driver, and 47% against 38%
at 32 GCDs. The reason is structural rather than incidental.

A finite-difference step communicates only with **nearest neighbours**: each
rank exchanges a face with each neighbour, and the volume of that exchange
falls as the subdomain shrinks. A distributed FFT communicates **all-to-all**:
the transpose between decomposition axes moves data between every pair of
ranks. As $p$ grows, nearest-neighbour traffic stays local while all-to-all
traffic grows, and the transpose comes to dominate the step.

::: {.callout-important}
## What this comparison does and does not say

The two Heat3D drivers solve the **same equation on the same machine**, so
comparing their *scaling behaviour* is legitimate, and the conclusion is that
halo exchange strong-scales better than a distributed transpose.

It does **not** follow that finite differences are the better choice. The two
runs are at different grid sizes ($512^3$ against $768^3$) and, more
importantly, the methods do not offer the same thing per step. The FD driver is
explicit and bound by @eq-cfl; the spectral driver is unconditionally stable
and can take a far larger timestep. Time-to-solution is the product of cost per
step and number of steps, and this chapter measures only the first factor.

Nor does it license comparing either Heat3D driver against `tungsten_hip`:
that is a different PDE with a different operator and a different amount of
work per step.
:::

## Where the 768³ curves stop being useful

All three fall below 50% efficiency by 24–32 GCDs. At $768^3$ on 32 GCDs each
rank holds roughly $14$ million cells, and for the spectral models the
transpose has become a substantial share of the step.

That is a statement about the grid, not about the code. The sections below
repeat the exercise at grids large enough to keep 16 nodes busy, and the
curves look quite different.

## Sixteen nodes {#sec-scal-16n}

Two studies at 128 GCDs, both on `tungsten_hip`, both with I/O off and
`wall_step` taken as the median over accepted steps after five warm-up steps,
using the **slowest rank** at each step — a step is not finished until every
rank is, so a mean across ranks would flatter an imbalanced run.

### Weak scaling: constant work per GCD {#sec-scal-weak}

The local block is held at exactly $2048\times2048\times16$ cells — 67.1
million per GCD — and $L_z$ grows with the rank count. OpenPFC decomposes into
$z$-slabs, so growing only $L_z$ keeps the local shape *exactly* constant
rather than approximately; a cubic ladder would need $N\propto P^{1/3}$ and
land on non-power-of-two transform sizes with unequal local blocks. The final
point is $2048^3$: **8.59 billion cells on 16 nodes**.

| nodes | GCDs | grid | wall/step | weak efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | $2048^2\times128$ | 204.5 ms | 100% |
| 2 | 16 | $2048^2\times256$ | 214.1 ms | 95.6% |
| 4 | 32 | $2048^2\times512$ | 315.9 ms | 64.7% |
| 8 | 64 | $2048^2\times1024$ | 398.1 ms | 51.4% |
| 16 | 128 | $2048^3$ | 412.4 ms | **49.6%** |

![Weak scaling of the tungsten PFC model to 16 nodes at constant 67.1 M cells
per GCD. Perfect weak scaling is the flat dashed line. The cost is paid almost
entirely between 2 and 4 nodes, where the all-to-all leaves the node and enters
the fabric; from 4 to 16 nodes a further $4\times$ in ranks costs only 15
percentage points.](figures/tungsten_weak_16n.svg){#fig-weak-16n}

The shape is more informative than the endpoint. Inside one node the transpose
is nearly free (95.6% at 2 nodes). Crossing onto the interconnect costs about
30 percentage points in one step. After that the curve is almost flat —
64.7% → 51.4% → 49.6% while the rank count quadruples — which is the
behaviour a distributed FFT should have once its all-to-all is already
inter-node.

### Strong scaling, and a divisibility trap {#sec-scal-strong16}

Fixed $1280^3$, 4 → 16 nodes.

| nodes | GCDs | $z$-planes per rank | wall/step | speedup | efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 32 | 40 | 296.8 ms | 1.00× | 100% |
| 8 | 64 | 20 | 174.5 ms | 1.70× | 85.0% |
| 10 | 80 | 16 | 141.2 ms | 2.10× | 84.1% |
| 12 | 96 | **13.33** | 258.7 ms | 1.15× | **38.3%** |
| 16 | 128 | 10 | 90.5 ms | 3.28× | **82.0%** |

![Strong scaling at $1280^3$. Filled points are rank counts that divide the
1280 $z$-planes evenly; the hollow point is the one that does not. Twelve
nodes is slower than eight *and* than ten — the same problem runs 1.8× faster
on 10 nodes than on 12.](figures/tungsten_strong_1280.svg){#fig-strong-1280}

**82% efficiency at 16 nodes** over a $4\times$ range in ranks, against a
$768^3$ curve that fell below 50% by four nodes. The model was simply too
small before.

The 12-node point is not noise. $1280 = 2^8\cdot5$ divides 32, 64, 80 and 128
exactly, giving 40, 20, 16 and 10 planes per rank, but $1280/96 = 13.33$: some
ranks get 13 planes and some 14, and every step waits for the slowest. The
10-node run was added specifically to test that explanation — $1280/80 = 16$
exactly — and it lands back on the curve at 84.1%. **On a slab-decomposed
spectral code, choose a rank count that divides the slab axis.** It is worth
more than a node.

### A memory boundary worth knowing {#sec-scal-memory}

$2048^3$ **cannot run below 16 nodes at all.** The strong-scaling ladder was
first attempted at that size and was OOM-killed at 32, 64 and 96 GCDs,
surviving only at 128. The kill is host-side rather than device-side: sampled
`MaxRSS` per task was 6.7–7.1 GB for the runs that died against 5.5 GB for the
one that lived, which points at a transient spike during transform setup that
the sampler does not catch. The practical rule from the sizing sweep is about
115 bytes per cell for this stack, and roughly 67 million cells per GCD is the
largest that reliably fits — which is exactly the weak-scaling design point
above.

## Spectral against finite difference {#sec-scal-methods}

@sec-heat3d is the one application carrying both a spectral and a
finite-difference solver for the same PDE, with a GPU twin of each and a
runtime `fd_order`. That makes it the only place in this report where the two
methods can be compared without changing anything else.

![Left: what one step costs on the same grid and hardware, the only difference
being the spatial operator. Right: how each method strong-scales to 16 nodes.
The panels answer different questions — cheap per step is not the same as
cheap per unit accuracy, which is @sec-scal-accuracy.](figures/heat3d_method_comparison.svg){#fig-method-comparison}

### Cost at equal grid

$1024^3$ on one node:

| method | wall/step | relative to FD-2 |
|---|---|---|
| FD, order 2 | 6.73 ms | 1.0× |
| FD, order 4 | 11.46 ms | 1.7× |
| FD, order 6 | 15.01 ms | 2.2× |
| FD, order 8 | 18.64 ms | 2.8× |
| FD, order 12 | 24.69 ms | 3.7× |
| **spectral** | **213.82 ms** | **31.8×** |

Finite-difference cost grows roughly linearly in stencil width, as the flop
count and halo depth do. The spectral step costs 32 times a second-order step
and still 8.7 times a twelfth-order one, which is the price of two global
transforms and the all-to-all between them.

### Scaling at equal grid

$1536^3$, 4 → 16 nodes. $1536 = 2^9\cdot3$ divides 32, 64, 96 and 128 exactly,
so the divisibility effect of @sec-scal-strong16 cannot contaminate this
comparison.

| method | 4 nodes | 8 | 12 | 16 | efficiency at 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| spectral | 283.4 ms | 168.0 | 112.8 | 85.0 | 83.3% |
| FD-2 | 5.91 ms | 2.99 | 2.11 | 1.73 | **85.3%** |
| FD-8 | 15.66 ms | 8.45 | 6.07 | 4.86 | 80.5% |

The expected result was that the spectral all-to-all would scale visibly worse
than a local stencil. **It does not.** All three land within five percentage
points of each other at 16 nodes. At $1536^3$ on 128 GCDs each rank still
holds 28 million cells, so the transpose has not yet become the dominant term;
the crossover where it would is beyond the range measured here. FD-8 scales
slightly *worse* than FD-2, which is the wider halo showing up.

### Accuracy, and where each operator is the cheaper way to get it {#sec-scal-accuracy}

@sec-heat3d's order-convergence study measures the third axis for one field:
every design order from 2 to 12 recovers its order, and the spectral operator
is exact to round-off. That study evolves a **single Fourier mode**, which is
the most favourable case a high-order stencil can be handed — its error
constant multiplies a high derivative that one smooth mode barely has. Read
literally it says FD-4 reaches $L^2 = 10^{-6}$ at $N=129$ for 0.02 ms per step
against the spectral path's 214 ms, and earlier versions of this chapter
declined to turn that into a recommendation for exactly that reason.

The question is now answered for fields of arbitrary spectral content, by
`heat3d_spectral_content_study`.

#### Why a closed form exists, and what $f$ means

`heat3d` solves $\partial_t u = D\nabla^2 u$ on a periodic box. That is linear
and constant-coefficient, so every operator in sight is diagonal in the
discrete Fourier basis and each mode evolves independently: the true PDE
decays mode $\mathbf k$ as $e^{-D|\mathbf k|^2t}$, the semi-discrete FD system
as $e^{D\lambda_p(\mathbf k)t}$ with the stencil's own symbol $\lambda_p$, and
the spectral operator uses $-|\mathbf k|^2$ itself — so its spatial error is
*identically zero*, not merely small. By Parseval the $L^2$ error of **any**
initial field is then a closed-form sum over that field's own spectrum. No
simulation is needed to draw the map; simulations are needed to check it, and
that is done below.

The initial condition is a Gaussian, whose width sweeps the spectrum
continuously from "everything at low $k$" to "content against Nyquist". The
one parameter is stated precisely:

> $f$ is the fraction of the Nyquist wavenumber at which the initial
> **amplitude** spectrum has fallen to $10^{-3}$ of its peak.

So $f = 0.2$ is a smooth blob on a grid several times finer than it needs, and
$f = 0.9$ is a field whose content runs right up to the grid scale. The field
is diffused for a dimensionless time $\tau = D t k_c^2 = 1$, i.e. until the
content-edge mode has decayed by $1/e$; over $\tau \in [0.5, 2]$ every number
below moves by less than a factor two, and the crossover does not depend on
$\tau$ at all. The map turns out to be independent of the grid $N$ as well
(pinned in `test_heat3d_spectral_content.cpp`), which is what makes $f$ — and
not a resolution — the right axis.

![Left: the $L^2$ error of each FD order against the fraction of Nyquist the
field's content reaches. The spectral operator is exact for every $f$, so it
is the $x$ axis rather than a curve. Stars mark where each order stops being
the cheaper route to a fixed accuracy. Right: the same statement priced, using
the measured per-step costs and an $N^3$ model — crossing the dashed line is
the result.](figures/heat3d_spectral_content.svg){#fig-spectral-content}

#### The crossover

Since $k_c$ is fixed by the physics, a method that tolerates content only up
to $f^*$ of Nyquist needs $N \propto 1/f^*$. **Assuming the cost of a fixed
number of steps scales as $N^3$**, the equal-accuracy cost of FD order $p$ is
$c_p/(f^*_p)^3$ against $c_\mathrm{spec}$, and the whole comparison collapses
to one line:

$$\text{FD-}p\ \text{is cheaper} \iff f^*_p(\varepsilon) > \sqrt[3]{c_p / c_\mathrm{spec}}.$$

That threshold is *pure cost arithmetic* — no numerics enter it. With the
per-step costs measured above it is remarkably narrow:

| order | per-step cost | crossover fraction | $L^2$ where it ties spectral |
|---|---|---|---|
| FD-2 | 6.73 ms | 0.316 | $1.4\times10^{-3}$ |
| FD-4 | 11.46 ms | 0.377 | $1.1\times10^{-4}$ |
| FD-6 | 15.01 ms | 0.413 | $1.7\times10^{-5}$ |
| FD-8 | 18.64 ms | 0.443 | $4.3\times10^{-6}$ |
| FD-12 | 24.69 ms | 0.487 | $6.5\times10^{-7}$ |

The reason the thresholds are so close together despite a 32× spread in
per-step cost is the cube root: **a 32× cheaper step buys only
$32^{1/3} = 3.2\times$ in grid spacing.** The per-step table, read on its own,
badly overstates how much protection finite differences have.

Priced out against a ladder of accuracy targets (spectral $= 1$):

| target $L^2$ | FD-2 | FD-4 | FD-6 | FD-8 | FD-12 | cheapest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $10^{-2}$ | **0.051** | 0.054 | 0.070 | 0.087 | 0.115 | FD-2 |
| $10^{-3}$ | 1.7 | 0.17 | 0.10 | **0.090** | 0.115 | FD-8 |
| $10^{-4}$ | 54 | 1.1 | 0.38 | 0.27 | **0.21** | FD-12 |
| $10^{-5}$ | $1.7\times10^{3}$ | 6.1 | 1.3 | 0.71 | **0.45** | FD-12 |
| $10^{-6}$ | $5.4\times10^{4}$ | 34 | 4.2 | 1.8 | **0.89** | FD-12 |
| $10^{-7}$ | $1.7\times10^{6}$ | 194 | 14 | 4.4 | 1.7 | **spectral** |
| $10^{-8}$ | $3.2\times10^{7}$ | $1.1\times10^{3}$ | 43 | 11 | 3.1 | **spectral** |
| $10^{-10}$ | — | $3.5\times10^{4}$ | 435 | 60 | 10 | **spectral** |

Three things follow, and they are the recommendation the chapter previously
could not give.

**Loose tolerances belong to finite differences, by a wide margin.** At
$10^{-2}$ FD-2 costs a twentieth of the spectral path, and the *lowest* order
is the right one — going higher only pays for accuracy nobody asked for. Most
of what these applications are used for lives here.

**The crossover is at $L^2 \approx 6\times10^{-7}$, and it belongs to FD-12.**
For any target tighter than that, no finite-difference order in the shipped
table is the cheaper way to reach it. The transition is not sharp in cost:
FD-12 is still 0.89× at $10^{-6}$ and 1.7× at $10^{-7}$. It *is* sharp in
which order to pick — the optimal order climbs from 2 to 8 to 12 between
$10^{-2}$ and $10^{-4}$ and then runs out of table.

**Broadband fields belong to the spectral path regardless of tolerance.** The
crossover fractions sit between a third and a half of Nyquist, so a field
whose content genuinely reaches the grid scale is already past every one of
them. At $f = 0.5$ the *best* stencil here manages $8.6\times10^{-7}$, and at
$f = 0.9$ it manages $2.2\times10^{-4}$ — those are the floors, not the costs
of reaching something better. This is not a hypothetical regime: at the
dealias-safe spacing of @sec-tungsten-dealias, six points per lattice period,
the crystal's third harmonic sits *exactly* on Nyquist, i.e. $f = 1$.

Two caveats on the arithmetic, both pointing the same way. The $N^3$ model
counts a fixed number of steps, which is generous to finite differences:
`heat3d_fd` is explicit, so its stable $\Delta t$ also falls as $\Delta x^2$
while `heat3d_spectral` is unconditionally stable, and at fixed physical end
time the FD refinement penalty is nearer $N^5$. And the per-step costs are
measured at $1024^3$ on 8 GCDs; the spectral step's all-to-all would degrade
relative to a local stencil at much larger rank counts than @sec-scal-methods
reaches. Every crossover above is therefore a *lower* bound on how often the
spectral path wins.

#### Validation

A semi-analytic result nobody checked is a guess with more decimal places, so
ten points on the map were re-measured by running the shipped FD stack for
real — the same `pfc::data::Field`, `pfc::comm::HaloExchange` and
`pfc::gradient::FDGradient<HeatGrads>` the production driver uses — and
comparing against the exact solution of the same sampled field. Classical RK4
is used in time rather than the driver's forward Euler, because the quantity
under test is a spatial error as small as $10^{-8}$ that Euler's $O(\Delta t)$
would swamp; each point is run twice, at $n$ and $2n$ steps, and the two
agreeing is the evidence that $\Delta t$ is not what is being measured.

| order | $N$ | $f$ | predicted | measured | measured/predicted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 64 | 0.30 | $1.278755\times10^{-3}$ | $1.278755\times10^{-3}$ | 1.0000000000 |
| 2 | 64 | 0.60 | $5.049084\times10^{-3}$ | $5.049084\times10^{-3}$ | 1.0000000000 |
| 4 | 64 | 0.30 | $4.375440\times10^{-5}$ | $4.375440\times10^{-5}$ | 1.0000000003 |
| 4 | 64 | 0.60 | $6.410647\times10^{-4}$ | $6.410647\times10^{-4}$ | 1.0000000000 |
| 6 | 64 | 0.40 | $1.383657\times10^{-5}$ | $1.383657\times10^{-5}$ | 1.0000000000 |
| 8 | 64 | 0.30 | $2.193288\times10^{-7}$ | $2.193288\times10^{-7}$ | 1.0000000037 |
| 8 | 64 | 0.60 | $3.864972\times10^{-5}$ | $3.864972\times10^{-5}$ | 1.0000000000 |
| 12 | 64 | 0.40 | $7.844075\times10^{-8}$ | $7.844075\times10^{-8}$ | 0.9999999963 |
| 12 | 64 | 0.60 | $5.541376\times10^{-6}$ | $5.541376\times10^{-6}$ | 1.0000000000 |
| 4 | 96 | 0.30 | $4.375440\times10^{-5}$ | $4.375440\times10^{-5}$ | 1.0000000003 |

**Prediction and measurement agree to between eight and ten significant
figures at every point**, on both sides of the crossover, with the worst
disagreement $3.7\times10^{-9}$ relative. The residual is round-off plus the
leftover RK4 term: doubling the step count on that worst point takes it from
$3.7\times10^{-9}$ to $5.6\times10^{-10}$, which is the temporal part going
away and leaving round-off behind. The last row is
the same $f$ on a different grid, which is the $N$-independence of the map
showing up in the runs and not only in the arithmetic. The full table,
including the doubled-step repeat of every point, is committed as
`data/heat3d_spectral_content_validation.csv`.

#### What this settles and what it does not

It settles the **linear** question completely, and only that. The heat
equation has no nonlinear term, so nothing here says anything about aliasing:
a spectral method applied to a cubic nonlinearity folds unresolved product
modes back into the solution, which is a different failure with a different
remedy (the $2/3$ mask) and is measured separately in @sec-tungsten-dealias.
Nor does it cover boundary conditions — everything above is periodic, where
the spectral operator is at its best — or any cost that is not per-step wall
time.

What it does cover transfers directly, because the crossover threshold is cost
arithmetic and the error map is a property of the field's spectrum: for any
constant-coefficient operator on a periodic box, compare the fraction of
Nyquist your field's content reaches against the cube root of the per-step
cost ratio, and that is your answer.

## Coverage and gaps

| Application | Scaling measured |
|---|---|
| @sec-tungsten | **Yes** — strong 1–128 GCDs ($768^3$, $1280^3$); weak 8–128 GCDs to $2048^3$ |
| @sec-heat3d (spectral HIP) | **Yes** — 1–32 GCDs ($768^3$); 32–128 GCDs ($1536^3$) |
| @sec-heat3d (FD HIP) | **Yes** — 1–32 GCDs ($512^3$); 32–128 GCDs ($1536^3$, orders 2 and 8) |
| @sec-aluminum | No |
| @sec-cahn-hilliard, @sec-thin-film, @sec-surface-diffusion, @sec-kawahara, @sec-ehd-film | No |
| @sec-higher-order-pfc | No — CPU/GPU agreement checked at 1 and 2 GCDs only |
| @sec-gradient-elasticity | No — not a time-stepping problem |
| @sec-wave2d, @sec-allen-cahn, @sec-kobayashi | No |

The unmeasured spectral applications share the ETD stack with @sec-tungsten
and would be expected to behave similarly at equal grid size, but that
expectation has not been tested and no curve is claimed for them.

Two gaps this section used to name are now closed. The weak-scaling one
(@sec-scal-weak): the tungsten model is measured to 16 nodes at constant work
per GCD, ending on 8.59 billion cells. And the accuracy one
(@sec-scal-accuracy): cost at equal accuracy is now measured for fields of
arbitrary spectral content, not just for a single smooth mode, and validated
against real runs to eight significant figures.

Two gaps remain, named explicitly:

* There is **no LUMI-C CPU control**, so the report still cannot say what the
  GPU path buys over CPU at equal node count.
* The **memory boundary is characterised but not diagnosed**
  (@sec-scal-memory). $2048^3$ is known to need 16 nodes, and the failure is
  known to be host-side, but the transient allocation responsible has not been
  traced.
